questions.q: « Tu vois le livre ? — Oui, je ___ vois. »
questions.why: Livre is masculine singular and it is a direct object, so le. And it lands before the verb, not after it: je le vois.

questions.q: Complete: « Tu connais Marie ? — Oui, je ___ connais. »
questions.why: Connaître takes its object with no preposition, so this is a direct object: la for a feminine person. Before a vowel it would elide to l'.

questions.q: Replace the object: « Il achète les billets. » → « Il ___ achète. »
questions.why: Les covers both genders in the plural for direct objects. The indirect plural would be leur, with no -s on the pronoun.

questions.q: « Je parle à Marie. » → « Je ___ parle. »
questions.why: Parler à takes a preposition before the person, so this is indirect: lui, which serves both his and her. Only ils/elles switches to leur.

questions.q: Replace the object: « Nous téléphonons à nos amis. » → « Nous ___ téléphonons. »
questions.why: Téléphoner à takes à before the person even though English says phone someone with no to. Plural indirect object, so leur, never leurs.

questions.q: « J'écoute Marie. » → which pronoun replaces Marie?
questions.why: Écouter takes no preposition in French, so the object is direct: la, elided to l' before the vowel. English listen to is the trap.

questions.q: Type what you hear.
questions.why: Me elides to m' before a vowel, and like every object pronoun it sits in front of the verb.

questions.q: Build the sentence: I don't see him.
questions.why: In the negative the pronoun still hugs the verb, so it slots between ne and the verb. Ne le vois pas, never ne vois le pas.

questions.q: Build the sentence: I saw him.
questions.why: In a compound tense the pronoun goes before the auxiliary, not before the participle. Je l'ai vu, never j'ai le vu.

questions.q: Which is the correct positive command for « Give me the book » ?
questions.why: A positive command is the one place the pronoun follows the verb, hyphenated, and me becomes moi (te becomes toi).

questions.q: Complete the negative command: « Ne ___ lève pas ! » (Don't get up!)
questions.why: A negative command puts everything back in the normal order, before the verb, and the pronoun reverts to te, not toi. Compare lève-toi !

questions.q: « Viens avec ___. » (Come with me.)
questions.why: After a preposition French uses a stressed pronoun. Same set after c'est, standing alone, in comparisons, and joined by et.

questions.q: Complete: « — Je ne suis pas fatigué. — Moi ___ . » (Me neither.)
questions.why: Moi aussi answers a positive statement, moi non plus a negative one. Using moi aussi after a negative is a very common learner error.

questions.q: Say this out loud.
questions.why: With an infinitive the pronoun attaches to the infinitive, not to the conjugated verb: je vais le voir, not je le vais voir.

questions.q: What is the test for choosing le / la / les versus lui / leur? Name two verbs where English misleads you.
a: Ask whether the French verb takes à before the person. If yes, use lui / leur (parler à, dire à, donner à, demander à, répondre à, téléphoner à, écrire à). If no, use le / la / les. English misleads with écouter quelqu'un (listen to → je l'écoute), regarder quelqu'un (look at → je le regarde), attendre quelqu'un (wait for → je l'attends), and téléphoner à quelqu'un (phone someone → je lui téléphone).
questions.why: The choice is decided by the French preposition, never by the English one. Learning the à-verbs as a list is faster than reasoning it out each time.

questions.q: « On ___ au marché le samedi. »
questions.why: On always takes the third-person singular, the same form as il, even when it plainly means we. On va, never on vont.

questions.q: Rewrite with on: « Nous avons mangé à huit heures. » → « ___ a mangé à huit heures. »
questions.why: In speech on has almost entirely replaced nous as a subject. The verb stays singular either way: on a mangé, never on ont mangé.

questions.q: « On reste chez ___ ce soir. » — which stressed pronoun goes with on?
questions.why: The stressed form of on is soi: on reste chez soi, chacun pour soi. Nous would be right only if the subject itself were nous.

questions.q: On here means we, several men: « On est ___ de partir. » (content)
questions.why: The verb stays singular, est, but the adjective may agree with what on really stands for. Singular verb plus plural adjective looks wrong and is correct.

questions.q: Complete with the reflexive pronoun: « On ___ lève à sept heures. »
questions.why: On is a third-person subject, so it reflexes with se, exactly like il: on se lève, on s'habille.

questions.q: Build the sentence: I never answer him.
questions.why: Répondre takes an indirect object, so lui, and it goes before the verb, inside the ne … jamais.

questions.q: Build the sentence: I'm going to call her tomorrow.
questions.why: With an infinitive the pronoun attaches to the infinitive, not to the conjugated verb: je vais l'appeler, never je la vais appeler.

questions.q: Build the sentence: She doesn't know us.
questions.why: Nous is the direct object here, and like every object pronoun it sits between ne and the verb.
